Joshua Holmes: Holmes gives Georgia a 6-foot-6 quarterback with the arm strength to threaten every level of coverage. He can drive throws deep and reach windows that change how a defense has to defend the field. That combination gives him the upside of a franchise quarterback.
Kalen Johnson: Johnson is an elite press-man corner who can disrupt a receiver at the line and stay attached through the break. His physicality sets the tone, and his fluid hips let him match changes of direction. Ohio State has a potential shutdown defender it can trust on the perimeter.
Zach Carr: Carr gives Notre Dame a dominant interior defender who can collapse a pocket through the middle. At 323 pounds, he pairs overwhelming power with forceful hands that let him control first contact. That combination makes him the kind of tackle a professional front can build around.
Brad Eaton: Eaton brings advanced anticipation and a command of the pocket that lets Colorado attack before a coverage window fully opens. His leadership gives the offense a clear presence at quarterback. That blend of timing and command gives him the upside to lead a professional passing game.
Shane Ryan: Ryan delivers the ball accurately and processes coverage quickly enough to give Michigan an answer as the defense changes its look. His polish lets him find windows on time and place throws where receivers can use them. Those traits give him franchise quarterback upside.
Malik Doucette: Doucette gives LSU a receiver who can create space with electric footwork and finish the play with reliable hands. His instincts show up when he turns upfield and finds room to run. That combination makes him a featured option an offense can use to create explosive gains.
Xander Williams: Williams gives Utah a 6-foot-8 blindside protector with powerful hands and the strength to control contact. His size lets him take up space on the edge, and his power gives him the tools to hold it. That profile projects as a long-term foundation at left tackle.
Hali'a Nalani: Nalani gives USC a 6-foot-4 receiver who can separate vertically and track the ball naturally once it is in the air. His speed forces defenders to account for the deep throw, and his reach gives the quarterback a large window. He projects as a featured downfield target.
Jermaine Williams: Williams accelerates quickly out of a smooth release and can create vertical separation before coverage settles. Ohio State can use his speed to reach behind a secondary or clear space for another route. His ability to build a gap downfield makes him a dangerous deep target.
Evans brings elite short-area quickness and physical coverage to the slot for Ole Miss. He can react to sharp breaks and has the versatility to handle different matchups inside. Those traits give a defense an instinctive option against receivers who rely on quick separation.
